title: Organism-to-organism relations are the most important cause of organic change

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Organism-to-organism relations are the most important cause of organic change

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The most important cause of organic change is the mutual relation of organism to organism, in which the improvement of one form causes the improvement or extermination of others; this is almost independent of changes, even sudden ones, in physical conditions.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the most important of all causes of organic change is one which is almost independent of altered and perhaps suddenly altered physical conditions, namely, the mutual relation of organism to organism,—the improvement of one being entailing the improvement or the extermination of others

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIV, “Recapitulation and Conclusion”; section “Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history”. Scope: all organisms over geological time

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch14-06: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.50

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing data permit comparative tests in selected systems. The all-organism, all-time ranking of causes is underdetermined because interaction histories are sparse and confounded.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Partition trait change, diversification and extinction rates among models driven by biotic interactions versus physical environmental change across replicated fossil clades and modern radiations. Greater standardized explanatory contribution from biotic variables would support the comparative 'most important' claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Biotic and physical drivers covary and operate at different scales.

Global causal importance has no single natural metric.

Biotic interactions are poorly preserved and incompletely recorded.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.38
data existence: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.38
discriminating power: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.52

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A variance partition of organic change into biotic and physical correlates is a fair operationalization, and fossil occurrences plus paleoclimate series support it for the physical side. Deep-time interactions themselves are largely absent, so the biotic term is a proxy. Existing data can address the contrast for some intervals and do not securely rank the causes for all of geological time.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Partition rates of origination, extinction and phenotypic change through time into components associated with biotic variables and with physical variables such as climate, and ask which component is larger. The claim is confirmed if biotic context explains more organic change than concurrent physical change across timescales, and refuted if physical change dominates or the two are inseparable.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Climate, sea level and collecting intensity move together with apparent turnover, which confounds the partition.

Who interacted with whom is rarely fossilized, so biotic drivers are inferred from diversity patterns rather than observed.

Which factor looks stronger depends on the time bin, so a single 'most important' cause is sensitive to scale.
